lessons.title: Your First AI Assistant: What Chatbots Can and Can't Do
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Your First AI Assistant: What Chatbots Can and Can't Do

When ChatGPT launched in late 2022, it reached 100 million users in about two months — faster than any product in history. But most people still use it like a slightly better Google. This lesson fixes that: you'll learn what an AI chatbot actually is, what it's genuinely great at, and where it will confidently mislead you.

## What a chatbot really is

Tools like ChatGPT (OpenAI), Claude (Anthropic), Gemini (Google), and Microsoft Copilot are all built on something called a large language model. Forget the jargon — here's the useful mental model: the model was trained on a huge amount of text from books, websites, and documents, and it learned patterns in how humans write and reason. When you type a message, it generates the most likely helpful response, word by word.

That means two important things. First, it's not looking things up in a database the way Google does — it's composing an answer. Second, it's remarkably good at language tasks: writing, explaining, summarizing, translating, and brainstorming.

## What it's great at (with examples)

- **Drafting and rewriting.** "Write a polite email declining a meeting invitation because of a schedule conflict." You'll get a usable draft in seconds.
- **Explaining things.** "Explain how a mortgage escrow account works like I'm 12." Great for learning anything.
- **Summarizing.** Paste a long article and ask for the key points in five bullets.
- **Brainstorming.** "Give me 10 low-cost birthday party ideas for a 7-year-old who loves dinosaurs."
- **Practice and role-play.** "Pretend you're an interviewer for a warehouse job. Ask me one question at a time and give feedback on my answers."

## Where it falls short

This is the part most tutorials skip, and it's the part that will save you from embarrassment:

- **It can make things up.** This is called "hallucination." Ask for a little-known fact, a legal citation, or a medical detail, and it may invent something plausible-sounding and wrong. Rule: never trust factual claims you haven't verified, especially for anything important like health, law, or money.
- **Its knowledge has a cutoff.** Unless it has web browsing turned on, it doesn't know about recent events. A free-tier answer about "this week's news" is a guess.
- **It doesn't know your context.** It doesn't know your company's policies, your boss's preferences, or your voice — until you tell it in the conversation.
- **It's a confident intern, not an expert.** Treat its output as a strong first draft that you review, not a final answer you ship blindly.

## A word on privacy

Free chatbots may use your conversations to improve their models. Practical rule: never paste passwords, Social Security numbers, bank details, or confidential work documents into a public chatbot. For everyday learning and drafting, you're fine.

## Try it now

1. Open chat.openai.com, claude.ai, or gemini.google.com and create a free account.
2. Ask: "Explain compound interest in simple terms with a concrete example."
3. Then ask a follow-up: "Now show me what happens with $100 a month for 10 years."
4. Notice how follow-up questions build on the conversation — that's the superpower.

## ✅ Lesson checklist

- [ ] Created a free account on one AI chatbot (ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini)
- [ ] Asked it to explain something and then asked a follow-up question
- [ ] Asked it one factual question, then verified the answer with a web search
- [ ] Can name two things chatbots are great at and two things they're bad at

lessons.title: Prompting Basics: Getting Better Answers on Purpose
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Prompting Basics: Getting Better Answers on Purpose

The difference between a mediocre answer and a great one is almost always the prompt — the instructions you give. "Prompting" sounds technical, but it's really just learning to ask clearly and completely. This lesson gives you a simple formula.

## The 4-part prompt formula

Great prompts usually include four ingredients:

1. **Role** — who should the AI act as?
2. **Context** — what background does it need?
3. **Task** — what exactly should it do?
4. **Format** — what should the answer look like?

Watch the difference:

❌ Weak: "Write a cover letter."

✅ Strong: "You are a friendly career coach (role). I'm applying for an entry-level warehouse associate job in Gary, Indiana. I have 3 years of retail experience and I'm reliable and punctual (context). Draft a cover letter for me (task). Keep it under 150 words, three short paragraphs, professional but warm tone (format)."

The strong version gives you something you can actually use, usually on the first try.

## More examples you can steal

**Meal planning:**
"You are a budget-friendly meal planner. I cook for two adults, we eat chicken but no pork, and I want to spend under $80 a week on groceries. Plan 5 dinners for next week. Format: a numbered list, each with the meal name, 3 key ingredients, and estimated cost."

**Learning:**
"You are a patient tutor. I never studied statistics. Explain what a 'median' is, give one real-world example, then quiz me with one question."

**Work email:**
"You are my writing assistant. Here's a rough draft of an email to a client about a delayed shipment: [paste draft]. Rewrite it to be professional, apologetic but not groveling, and under 120 words."

## The follow-up is the real skill

Your first prompt gets you 70% of the way there. The magic is in iterating:

- "Make it shorter."
- "Make it sound more casual."
- "Give me 3 more options for the last paragraph."
- "Now turn this into a text message instead of an email."

Think of it as a conversation with a fast assistant, not a vending machine.

## Two pro techniques

**Give an example.** Show the style you want: "Write product descriptions in this style: [paste one example]. Now write one for a blue ceramic coffee mug."

**One job at a time.** Don't ask for a cover letter, a resume rewrite, and interview tips in one prompt. Split them up — each answer will be better.

## Common mistakes

- **Too vague:** "Tell me about marketing" gets you a textbook chapter. Say what it's for.
- **No format:** without format guidance you get walls of text. Ask for bullets, tables, or word limits.
- **Blind trust:** if the answer contains facts, dates, or numbers you'll act on, verify them. The AI is a drafter, not a fact-checker.

## ✅ Lesson checklist

- [ ] Rewrote one vague prompt using the Role + Context + Task + Format formula
- [ ] Practiced a follow-up: asked the AI to revise an answer twice
- [ ] Tried the "give an example" technique once
- [ ] Saved a go-to prompt template in your notes for something you do often

lessons.title: Writing Faster: Emails, Documents, and Summaries
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Writing Faster: Emails, Documents, and Summaries

Most adults spend hours a week writing emails, reports, and messages. AI won't replace your judgment, but it can take the blank-page dread out of writing. This lesson gives you three repeatable workflows.

## Workflow 1: From rough thoughts to polished email

You don't need a perfect draft — you need your raw thoughts. Try this:

1. Type your messy thoughts: "need to tell client johnson the shipment is late, truck broke down, will arrive thursday not tuesday, sorry, offer discount on next order"
2. Prompt: "Turn these notes into a professional email to a client. Apologetic but confident, under 150 words, with a clear subject line."
3. Read the draft, fix anything wrong (names, dates, details), and send.

The AI handles structure and tone; you handle facts. That division of labor is the whole game.

## Workflow 2: Tame long documents

Got a 20-page report, a long email thread, or dense terms and conditions? Don't read it all first:

- "Summarize this document in 5 bullet points I can read in 60 seconds."
- "What are the 3 most important deadlines or action items in this text?"
- "Explain this contract clause in plain English: [paste clause]"

Paste the text into the chat (ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini all accept long pastes; Claude handles especially long documents well). For PDFs, many chatbots now let you upload the file directly.

## Workflow 3: Match the tone

"Rewrite this so it sounds firm but polite" is one of the highest-value prompts in professional life. Others:

- "Make this more concise — cut it in half without losing the key points."
- "Make this warmer and friendlier."
- "Turn this paragraph into 3 bullet points for a slide."

## Tools that build this in

Beyond the chatbots themselves, AI writing help is now built into tools you may already use:

- **Grammarly** — rewrites sentences, adjusts tone, and checks clarity as you type; the free tier is genuinely useful.
- **Microsoft Copilot in Word/Outlook** — drafts and rewrites inside your documents and emails (requires a Microsoft 365 subscription).
- **Gemini in Gmail/Google Docs** — "Help me write" drafts emails and expands rough notes in Docs (Google Workspace).

You don't need all of them. Pick the one that lives where you already write.

## A note on voice

If everything you send starts sounding like a chatbot, dial it back: add "in my own voice, casual" to prompts, or just edit the draft. The goal is to sound like you on a good day, not like a robot.

## ✅ Lesson checklist

- [ ] Turned messy notes into a real email using Workflow 1
- [ ] Summarized one long document or article into 5 bullets
- [ ] Rewrote one message to change its tone
- [ ] Picked one writing tool (Grammarly, Copilot, or Gemini) to try for a week

lessons.title: Meetings and Spreadsheets: Let AI Do the Tedious Parts
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Meetings and Spreadsheets: Let AI Do the Tedious Parts

Two of the biggest time sinks at work — sitting through meetings and wrestling with spreadsheets — are exactly where AI helps most. Here's how to set both up.

## Part 1: Never take meeting notes again

AI meeting assistants join your video calls, transcribe everything, and produce a summary with action items. The main options:

- **Otter.ai** — free tier includes 300 transcription minutes a month; works with Zoom, Google Meet, and Teams.
- **Fireflies.ai** — similar; free tier covers limited meetings.
- **Zoom AI Companion** — built into Zoom; generates meeting summaries if your account has it enabled.
- **Microsoft Teams Copilot** — built into Teams for Microsoft 365 Copilot subscribers.

**Typical setup (using Otter as an example):**

1. Create a free account at otter.ai and connect your Google or Outlook calendar.
2. Toggle on "auto-join" — Otter joins scheduled meetings as a participant and records.
3. After the meeting, open the transcript. You'll see a summary, key topics, and action items with owners.
4. Skim the action items, fix anything misattributed, and paste them into your task list or an email.

**Two cautions:** tell attendees the meeting is being recorded (it's polite and sometimes legally required), and check your company's policy — some employers restrict third-party recording tools.

What you get back: instead of 45 minutes of notes, you get "Decisions: approved $2k budget. Action items: Maria sends vendor quote by Friday; James books the venue." Review it for 3 minutes and move on.

## Part 2: Spreadsheets without the formula pain

You don't need to memorize Excel formulas anymore. Describe what you want in plain English:

- "I have first names in column A and last names in column B. Give me an Excel formula to combine them with a space." → `=A2&" "&B2`
- "I have a list of sales in column C. What's the formula for the total of only the values over 100?" → `=SUMIF(C:C,">100")`

**The paste-and-ask method:** copy a few rows of your spreadsheet into ChatGPT or Claude and describe the result you want: "Here's sample data. I need a formula that finds the most recent order date for each customer." It will give you the formula and explain how it works — paste it into your sheet and test on a copy of your data first.

**Built-in helpers:** Google Sheets has a Gemini sidebar ("Help me organize" can build tables and generate formulas), and Excel's Copilot can analyze data and suggest charts if you have a subscription.

**Reality check:** always test AI-generated formulas on a copy of your data. A wrong formula applied to a real budget is worse than no formula. Verify the first few results by hand.

## ✅ Lesson checklist

- [ ] Signed up for one meeting assistant and connected your calendar (or noted your company's policy if restricted)
- [ ] Reviewed one AI meeting summary and corrected an action item
- [ ] Got an AI-generated formula working in a real spreadsheet
- [ ] Tested the formula on sample data before trusting it

lessons.title: Image and Creative Tools: Quick Graphics Without a Designer
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Image and Creative Tools: Quick Graphics Without a Designer

Sometimes you need a decent image fast — a slide background, a social media post, a blog header, a flyer. AI image generators can produce one from a text description in under a minute. This lesson shows you how to get usable results.

## The main tools

- **ChatGPT (with DALL-E)** — describe the image in chat; included in free and Plus tiers. Easiest starting point.
- **Microsoft Designer / Copilot** — free image generation powered by DALL-E; good for social posts.
- **Adobe Firefly** — built into Adobe Express and Photoshop; trained on licensed content, which matters for commercial use.
- **Canva's Magic Studio** — "Magic Media" generates images right inside Canva designs; great if you already make flyers or posts in Canva.
- **Midjourney** — runs through Discord; produces striking, artistic images but has a learning curve and no free tier.

Start with whichever you already have access to — for most people that's ChatGPT or Canva.

## How to describe what you want

Vague prompts give generic images. Include four things: **subject, style, colors/mood, composition.**

❌ "A coffee shop"

✅ "A cozy neighborhood coffee shop interior at golden hour, warm wood tones, a barista pouring latte art, photorealistic style, wide shot with empty space on the left for text"

More examples:

- "Flat vector illustration of a diverse team around a laptop, purple and teal color palette, minimalist, no text"
- "Watercolor painting of the Chicago skyline at sunset, soft pinks and oranges, panoramic"

Add "no text" when you don't want words in the image — AI still garbles text often.

## What it's good for (and not)

**Good for:** presentation backgrounds, blog headers, social media graphics, mockups and brainstorming visuals, flyers for community events.

**Not good for:** anything requiring accurate text in the image, realistic faces of real people, logos (it can't do precise brand work), or photos you claim are real.

## Know the limits

- **Hands, faces, and text** are the classic weak spots — zoom in and check before publishing.
- **Commercial use** varies by tool and plan; Firefly and paid tiers are generally safer for business use. Check the terms.
- **Disclose when it matters.** For a slide background, nobody cares. For anything presented as photography or representing real people, be upfront.

## ✅ Lesson checklist

- [ ] Generated 3 images from the same subject with increasingly detailed prompts — compared results
- [ ] Made one usable graphic (slide background, post, or flyer) with an AI image
- [ ] Checked the image at full size for garbled text or weird details
- [ ] Read the commercial-use terms for the tool you used
